title: Image Overlap
statement:
`img1` and `img2` are square `n x n` grids whose cells are each `0` or `1`. You may move one of the grids as a whole by any whole number of rows up or down and any whole number of columns left or right (rotations are not allowed), then lay it over the other grid. Any `1` that ends up outside the `n x n` frame disappears.

The **overlap** of a placement is the number of cells that hold `1` in both grids. Return the largest overlap you can get over all possible shifts, including no shift at all.
notes:
## Intuition

A shift is just a pair of offsets: how many rows and how many columns `img1` moves. With an `n x n` grid each offset ranges from `-(n - 1)` to `n - 1`; anything larger pushes every cell off the frame. That is only `(2n - 1)²` shifts, at most 3,481 for `n = 30`, so we can simply try every one and count the matching `1`s.

A faster-on-sparse-grids alternative pairs every `1` of `img1` with every `1` of `img2` and tallies the vector between them; the most frequent vector is the best shift. Both give the same answer.

## Approach

1. Let `n` be the side length and `best = 0`.
2. For every `rowShift` and `colShift` from `-(n - 1)` to `n - 1`, reset `count` to 0.
3. For each cell `(r, c)` of `img1`, its shifted position is `(r2, c2) = (r + rowShift, c + colShift)`. Skip it if that falls outside the grid.
4. If both `img1[r][c]` and `img2[r2][c2]` are `1`, add one to `count`.
5. After each shift, keep the larger of `best` and `count`. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`img1 = [[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,1,0]]`, `img2 = [[0,0,0],[0,1,1],[0,0,1]]`, so `n = 3` and both shifts run from `-2` to `2`. With no shift only cell `(1,1)` matches, so `count = 1`. With `rowShift = 1, colShift = 1`, `img1`'s ones at `(0,0)`, `(0,1)`, `(1,1)` land on `(1,1)`, `(1,2)`, `(2,2)`, all `1` in `img2` (the one at `(2,1)` falls off the bottom), so `count = 3`. No shift does better, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n⁴): `(2n - 1)²` shifts, each scanning up to `n²` cells.
- Space: O(1): only counters.

## Pitfalls

- Shifts go both ways: include negative offsets, not just `0..n-1`.
- Check both `r2` and `c2` against the frame before reading `img2`; out-of-range reads give `undefined`, and in Java or C they crash.
- Shifting `img1` over `img2` is enough: moving `img2` by the opposite offset gives the same overlap.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | side length of both grids |
| `best` | largest overlap found so far |
| `rowShift`, `colShift` | how far `img1` is moved down and right (negative means up or left) |
| `count` | overlap for the current shift |
| `r`, `c` | a cell of `img1` |
| `r2`, `c2` | where that cell lands in `img2` after the shift |

narration.2: Both grids share the same side length n.
narration.3: No placement has been counted yet, so the best overlap starts at 0.
narration.5: Try every vertical shift; beyond n - 1 in either direction every cell leaves the frame.
narration.6: For each vertical shift, try every horizontal shift too.
narration.7: Start a fresh tally for this shift.
narration.9: Row r of img1 lands on row r2 of img2.
narration.10: If that row is outside the frame, nothing on it can overlap...
narration.14: Column c of img1 lands on column c2 of img2.
narration.15: Count the cell when it stays inside the frame and both images hold a 1 there.
narration.16: One more overlapping 1 for this shift.
narration.20: Keep the larger of the best so far and this shift's overlap.
narration.23: Every shift has been tried; return the largest overlap.
